Q01.answer: They dropped speech recognition and kept the LCD screen. Speaker B said without the LCD 'we lose our whole concept', and Speaker A added that losing the screen would mean a lot of extra buttons; dropping speech also saved four Euros, as it had not been integrated yet.

Q02.answer: In meeting c they leaned towards a flexible, spongy (stress-ball type) rubber case, but in the final meeting they switched to a solid plastic case. The design was about four Euros over budget, mostly because of the LCD, and plastic cost nothing on the cost sheet while rubber cost two Euros a unit, so plastic let them keep the LCD.

changing it to plastic and a solid unit

Q03.answer: The titanium back was chosen in meeting c. In the final meeting Speaker B (Mike, the user interface designer) first proposed replacing it with titanium-coloured plastic, and Speaker D backed a hard plastic that looks like titanium rather than losing the LCD. The titanium was not kept: the project manager (A) said 'we have to dump our titanium'.

replace the titanium with

Q04.answer: They chose batteries combined with solar cells. When the costs were added up the design came to about twenty-two Euros against the 12.50 limit, the solar cell was named as what made it expensive, and it was left out (along with voice recognition) to reach 12.40 Euros.

Q05.answer: In meeting c they settled on a battery charged by kinetic movement (battery and kinetic combined); in the final meeting they ended with plain batteries only. The change was proposed by Speaker A, the project manager, who asked to skip the kinetic part because shaking the remote is not really innovative, and it also cut cost.

the energy, which uh turn out to be uh batteries

Q06.answer: The team agreed in meeting b that they wanted a feature to keep the remote from getting lost, but in the final meeting they dropped it ('decided not to worry about that for now'). The main objection came from Speaker C (Iain, user interface designer): it would be technically difficult because a lost remote is usually under the settee where an infrared signal cannot reach it, and it might be just a gimmick.

Q08.answer: Speaker D (Reissa, the marketing expert) raised RSI, repetitive strain injury, from pressing buttons and changing channels. The team responded by choosing soft rubber push-buttons on a rubber, double-curved case and marketing the remote as 'anti-RSI', the opposite of remotes that cause strain.

Q09.answer: At first they were working with a selling price of 25 Euros; later the project manager set a sales bracket of 35 to 50 Euros. Speaker D, who argued from the marketing side, pushed hardest for a high, exclusive price, first suggesting 89 Euros and then wholesale at 50 to 60 Euros as 'the Rolls Royce of remote controls'.

Q10.answer: They decided to design for elderly people, roughly sixty to eighty years old. The project manager (A) argued that new products are designed for younger people so they could focus on the elderly, Speaker C pointed to the big success of the mobile phone for the elderly, and the marketing expert (D) said it would be good for the company image and a good market.

Q12.answer: The voice-recognition finder was taken out of the final design because it pushed the cost over the budget; removing it brought the remote to about 12.35 Euros, and it was suggested as an optional upgrade for business-class customers. Speaker D said the object itself is so distinctive (bright fruit-and-vegetable colours) that it would be easy to locate anyway.

Q13.answer: Yes, speech recognition was in their final design (in the last meeting they confirmed it was still affordable and the four-Euro sample speaker was included). Their last reversal was in their third meeting (TS3004c): having said 'we just decide not to put it in', the project manager reversed seconds later with 'we just put it in, because it's a good feature'.

Q14.answer: Their final costing came to 8.20 Euros, well within the 12.50 budget. The speech (voice) recogniser that had been left pending cost research was not included in that total: the project manager realised there was no room for it in the financing and was unsure the remaining 4.30 Euros would cover it.

Q15.answer: Their first full costing came to 15.50 Euros against a limit of 12.50 Euros, three Euros over. They fixed it by removing the LCD display (the information could be shown on the TV instead), which brought it to 12.50.

Q16.answer: The project manager (A) favoured a small joystick, like the pointer on a laptop, for navigating. In the final costed design it was replaced by four ordinary push-buttons (up, down, left, right). To reach the 12.50 Euro budget they also gave up the special colour: the yellow case was counted as a normal colour, and the red and green buttons had to be the same colour as the rest.

button up, button down, button right, button left
No joystick. Push-buttons. No special colour

Q17.answer: The touch screen, provisionally chosen in meeting b, was dropped in their third meeting (ES2009c), where the project manager said they would omit the touch screen in favour of voice recognition, which they kept instead. The industrial designer (B, Nathan) estimated the touch screen would cost upwards of 17.50 Euros per remote.

In the next meeting she reported back that the remote would be just for television, not video, because otherwise it would become too complex.

Q25.answer: They dropped fruit and vegetable shapes and kept one comfortable, joystick-like shape (the 'broccoli' form won), showing the fruit theme through different colours named after fruits or printed fruit designs instead. Fruit shapes were uncomfortable or too big to hold, irregular shapes would cost more to produce, and different colours were much cheaper than different shapes.

Q18.answer: In meeting b they planned a simple whistle-back (then clap-back) function, so the remote answers a whistle or clap when lost. In meeting c this became the company's small speech-recognition unit used only to find the remote, answering a spoken message like 'where are you remote'. Speaker C (Louisa, the user interface designer) suggested marketing it to buyers as a finder function rather than as a speech-recognition feature, and the project manager agreed.

In the final meeting it was replaced by plastic, suggested by Speaker B (the user interface designer) during the costing, since plastic was free on the cost sheet.

Speaker D (Courtney) preferred triple-A batteries because they would make the remote lighter (and the project manager noted lithium is more expensive). In the final costing they chose a single lithium battery.

Q23.answer: They kept their headline features, voice recognition and the LCD display (both chosen in meeting c). To get under the 12.50 budget they removed the expensive sample speaker, replacing its talking feedback and locator with a simple beeper, and swapped the scroll wheel for two plain up/down push-buttons on the side.

The team then decided to drop the LCD, since without it the remote would be cheaper, simpler to use and look better.
